faq.question: What can Cloud Nest help with?
faq.answer: We cover website design and development, brand design and guidelines, digital marketing, paid advertising, and SEO. You can start with a single service or discuss a connected project.

faq.question: How much will my project cost?
faq.answer: Pricing depends on the scope, complexity, content, and support you need. The Launch, Grow, and Scale options are starting points for a conversation. A project quote should set out deliverables, costs, and payment milestones before work begins.

faq.question: How long does a website take?
faq.answer: The timeline depends on the number of pages, functionality, available content, and review rounds. We agree on milestones after understanding your project, so you know what is needed and when.

faq.question: Can you improve an existing website or brand?
faq.answer: Yes. Share your current website or brand materials and what you want to improve. We can discuss a focused update, a redesign, or a broader refresh based on what already works.

faq.question: Will the website work on mobile?
faq.answer: Responsive layouts are part of our website service. Navigation, text, images, and forms are designed to adapt to phones, tablets, and desktop screens.

faq.question: What should I prepare before getting started?
faq.answer: Bring your business goals, audience, any existing brand assets, a few references, and an idea of your budget and timeline. If the brief is still taking shape, start with the problem you want to solve.

blog.title: Before you redesign your website, ask these five questions
blog.excerpt: A redesign is a chance to make your website more useful. Before choosing colours or collecting references, write down what needs to change. Is the offer unclear? Is it difficult to enquire? Does the website no longer reflect your business? A clear problem gives the project a purpose.
blog.body:
Start with the problem, not the mood board.
A redesign is a chance to make your website more useful. Before choosing colours or collecting references, write down what needs to change. Is the offer unclear? Is it difficult to enquire? Does the website no longer reflect your business? A clear problem gives the project a purpose.

1. Who is the website for?
Describe the people you want to reach, what they need, and what they may already know. A first-time customer needs a different introduction from an existing client. Use that distinction to decide what belongs on the page.

2. What should visitors do next?
Choose the most useful next step for each page: understand a service, compare options, or start a conversation. Keep that action easy to find and explain what happens after someone takes it.

3. What content can you bring?
Gather your service descriptions, photography, brand files, and answers to common questions. Identify anything that needs to be written or created. Content is part of the project, not something to squeeze in at the end.

4. What should you keep?
Review the existing website before replacing it. Keep useful information, clear language, and familiar routes that still serve your audience. A redesign can build on what works.

5. How will you judge the result?
Set a practical goal you can review after launch. That might be fewer confused enquiries, a simpler booking process, or a clearer explanation of your services. Agree on the goal before judging the design.

blog.title: A good brand is more than a beautiful logo
blog.excerpt: A logo is an important part of a brand, but it rarely appears alone. It sits next to words, photographs, colour, typography, and layout. Those choices need to feel like they belong to the same business.
blog.body:
Think in systems.
A logo is an important part of a brand, but it rarely appears alone. It sits next to words, photographs, colour, typography, and layout. Those choices need to feel like they belong to the same business.

Start with what you want to communicate.
Write down what your business does, who it serves, and how you want people to describe it. Be specific. “Clear and approachable” gives a designer a more useful direction than “make it premium” on its own.

Give every element a job.
Choose type that suits the way your business communicates. Use colour with a clear hierarchy. Decide how images should feel, and how headings should sound. A useful identity makes those decisions easier to repeat.

Create guidelines people can actually use.
A brand guide should answer practical questions: which logo belongs on a dark background, how much space it needs, which colours and type styles to use, and what to avoid. Real examples make the rules easier to follow.

Leave room for the brand to grow.
Test the system across a website, a social post, and a simple document. It should feel connected without making every piece identical. The aim is a recognisable identity that can adapt to the work ahead.

blog.title: How to turn a big idea into a useful project brief
blog.excerpt: A good brief starts a useful conversation. It explains what you are trying to achieve and gives your creative or development partner enough context to ask better questions.
blog.body:
You do not need all the answers.
A good brief starts a useful conversation. It explains what you are trying to achieve and gives your creative or development partner enough context to ask better questions.

Describe the problem in one paragraph.
Explain what happens today, who it affects, and what you want to improve. Keep the focus on the need before choosing a particular feature or technology.

Separate essentials from possibilities.
List what the first version must do, then keep future ideas in a separate list. This makes it easier to discuss a practical starting scope without losing the bigger picture.

Share references with a reason.
When you share a website or visual reference, explain what you like about it. It might be the navigation, tone, clarity, or use of space. A reference becomes more useful when your partner understands the reason behind it.

Be open about constraints.
Include your intended launch date, budget range if known, available content, and who will review the work. Mention existing systems that need to be connected. These details help shape a realistic plan.

End with a definition of success.
Describe what a useful finished result would let you or your customers do. That shared definition gives both sides something concrete to work towards.
